query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Modifying the chemical composition of an equiatomic high-entropy alloy, for example by deviating the FeCoNiTi stoichiometry to adjust the balance between magnetic and non‐magnetic elements, will enhance the magnetocaloric response near its magnetic phase transition.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near‐equiatomic FeCoNiTi high-entropy alloy exhibiting standard magnetocaloric behavior under baseline conditions.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the alloy’s chemical composition by increasing or decreasing the concentration of specific magnetic elements.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under controlled temperatures and applied magnetic fields over a broad compositional range.
generation.structural_mediator: Altered magnetic domain structure and phase fraction changes that result from lattice distortion due to compositional modifications.
generation.mechanism: Adjusting the relative concentrations of magnetic elements changes the magnetic interaction strengths and shifts the Curie temperature, thereby increasing the magnetic entropy change during magnetization/demagnetization cycles.
generation.predicted_outcome: An enhanced magnetocaloric effect, as evidenced by a larger entropy change and adiabatic temperature change near the phase transition compared to the baseline composition.
generation.baseline: The original magnetocaloric performance of an equiatomic (or standard composition) FeCoNiTi alloy prepared by arc melting and rapid quenching.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected only within the compositional range that preserves the high-entropy single-phase structure; excessive deviation may induce deleterious phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise compositional ratios that yield the optimal magnetocaloric enhancement remain uncertain and will need to be identified via systematic experimental mapping.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FeCoNiTi-based high-entropy alloys with systematically varied compositions. Subject these samples to controlled magnetometry and calorimetric measurements over a temperature range encompassing the magnetic phase transition. Compare the magnetocaloric properties, specifically the magnetic entropy change (ΔS_M) and adiabatic temperature change (ΔT_ad), of the modified alloys to those of the baseline equiatomic alloy.
measurements: DC magnetization as a function of temperature and field
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to capture heat flow around the phase transition
Direct measurements of adiabatic temperature change under applied magnetic fields
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the modified compositions show a statistically significant increase in magnetic entropy change or adiabatic temperature change compared to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis that composition tuning improves the magnetocaloric performance will be rejected.

The as-cast polycrystalline sample (1.5 g) of FeCoNiTi was prepared through a homemade arc furnace. The elemental components, Fe chips (Kojundo Chemical Laboratory, 99.9%), Co chips (Kojundo Chemical Laboratory, 99.9%), Ni wire (Soekawa Rikagaku, 99.9%), and Ti wire (Nilaco, 99.9%), were employed in a fixed atomic ratio of Fe:Co:Ni:Ti = 1:1:1:1. These constituent elements were remelted several times on a water-cooled Cu hearth and flipped each time to ensure homogeneity under Ar atmosphere. The finalization of the sample preparation involved rapid quenching on the water-cooled Cu hearth.

Room temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were captured utilizing an X-ray diffractometer (XRD-7000L, Shimadzu) with Cu–Kα radiation in the Bragg–Brentano geometry. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
